procedural_history.originating_court: Learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, who forwarded the matter to the Chief Judge, City Sessions Court, Calcutta.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 7th April, 2022 (likely an order of the Chief Judge, City Sessions Court, Calcutta, since the High Court interfered with it).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court interfered with the order dated 7th April, 2022, and allowed the petition filed by the respondent (order dated 11th May, 2023).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of West Bengal appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order dated 11th May, 2023. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court of sessions was entitled to entertain an application for extension of the period of remand in terms of the proviso to Section 43D (5) of the UAPA when no special court had been notified by the State of West Bengal under Section 22(1) of the National Investigating Agency Act, 2008.

facts: The case involved offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA), which were being investigated by the State police in West Bengal.
The State of West Bengal had not exercised its power under Section 22(1) of the National Investigating Agency (NIA) Act, 2008, to constitute or notify a Special Court for the trial of such offences.
The investigating agency filed an application before the Court of Sessions to extend the period of the accused's detention beyond 90 days, as permitted under Section 43D of the UAPA.
law: Section 22(3) of the NIA Act states that until a Special Court is constituted by the State Government, the Court of Sessions of the division where the offence was committed shall have the jurisdiction and all the powers of a Special Court under the Act.

The proviso to Section 43D(2) of the UAPA gives the 'Court' the power to authorize the detention of an accused beyond the standard 90-day period, up to 180 days, if the investigation cannot be completed within that time.
application: The Supreme Court determined that since the investigation was conducted by the State police, Section 22 of the NIA Act was the applicable provision for jurisdiction.
The Court noted the undisputed fact that the State of West Bengal had not designated a Special Court under Section 22(1).

Applying the legal provision in Section 22(3) of the NIA Act, the Court found that this subsection acts as a 'deeming provision'. In the absence of a notified Special Court, the local Court of Sessions is legally vested with all the jurisdiction and powers of a Special Court.

Therefore, the Court of Sessions for the relevant division had the authority to exercise all powers conferred on a Special Court, including the power under Section 43D of the UAPA to extend the period of remand.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and held that the Court of Sessions was entitled to entertain the application for extension of the remand period. This was because, by virtue of Section 22(3) of the NIA Act, the Court of Sessions functions as the Special Court with all its attendant powers until the State Government formally constitutes one.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Chief Judge, City Sessions Court, Calcutta had the jurisdiction to pass the order dated 7th April, 2022.

facts: A case involving offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) was forwarded to the Chief Judge, City Sessions Court, Calcutta.
The Chief Judge passed an order in the matter on April 7, 2022.
law: A Special Court had been constituted for the State of West Bengal by the Central Government via a Gazette Notification dated April 29, 2011.
When a Special Court is notified and functioning, it has exclusive jurisdiction to handle cases involving offences under the UAPA.
Once UAPA offences are added to a case, other courts, such as the Magistrate's Court or the City Sessions Court, are denuded of their power to proceed in the matter.
application: The Supreme Court considered that a designated and functioning Special Court already existed in West Bengal to try UAPA cases.
Because this Special Court had been established, the Chief Judge of the City Sessions Court did not have the legal authority to preside over the case or issue orders related to the UAPA offences.
The proceedings before the Chief Judge were therefore considered vitiated and without jurisdiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the Chief Judge, City Sessions Court, Calcutta, did not have the jurisdiction to pass the order dated April 7, 2022. The Court reasoned that since a Special Court had already been constituted in West Bengal for UAPA cases, all orders passed by the Chief Judge pertaining to these offences were illegal and without jurisdiction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order dated 07.04.2022, whereby the Chief Judge cum City Sessions Court permitted the addition of the offences under Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 to the case suffer from any illegality or infirmity; whether the extension of remand by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate beyond the period of 90 days was illegal.

facts: An FIR was initially registered against the accused under various sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The Investigating Officer later filed an application to add more serious offences under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA).
On 07.04.2022, the Chief Judge cum City Sessions Court permitted the addition of the UAPA offences to the case.
Following this, the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) extended the judicial remand of the accused beyond the standard 90-day period.
law: Section 22(3) of the National Investigation Agency (NIA) Act, 2008, grants the Sessions Court the power and jurisdiction to deal with such cases.
Section 2(1)(d) of the UAPA defines a 'Court' as including both a normal criminal court (like a Magistrate's court) and a Special Court constituted under the NIA Act.

Section 43D(2) of the UAPA allows for the detention of an accused to be extended beyond 90 days and up to 180 days, but this power can only be exercised by the Sessions Court or the Special Court, not the Magistrate.
application: The Supreme Court first analyzed the legality of the order adding the UAPA charges. It determined that under Section 22(3) of the NIA Act, the Chief Judge cum City Sessions Court had the proper jurisdiction to hear the application and permit the addition of the UAPA offences. Therefore, the order dated 07.04.2022 was held to be valid and without any illegality.

Next, the Court examined the extension of remand by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM). It clarified that while a Magistrate has the jurisdiction to deal with the remand of an accused under the UAPA, this authority is limited to the initial 90-day period.
The Court found that any extension of remand beyond 90 days requires an express order from the Sessions Court or a Special Court, as mandated by Section 43D(2) of the UAPA.
Consequently, the CMM's action of extending the remand beyond 90 days was without jurisdiction and was declared "grossly illegal" by the Supreme Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided the issue in two parts. It held that the order dated 07.04.2022, which added the UAPA offences, was legal and valid because the City Sessions Court had the jurisdiction to pass it. However, it concluded that the extension of the accused's remand beyond 90 days by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate was "grossly illegal," as only the Sessions Court or a Special Court has the authority to grant such an extension under the UAPA.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court of sessions was entitled to entertain an application for extension of the period of remand in terms of the proviso to Section 43D (5) of the UAPA when no special court had been notified by the State of West Bengal under Section 22(1) of the National Investigating Agency Act, 2008.
appellant_arguments: As the case was investigated by the State police and no Special Court had been constituted by the State Government under Section 22(1) of the NIA Act, the Sessions Court having jurisdiction was seized of the exclusive jurisdiction to try the offences as per Section 22(3) of the NIA Act.
respondent_arguments: The view taken by the High Court (which found the Sessions Court lacked jurisdiction) was the only permissible and legal view.
The respondent referred to a Gazette Notification dated 29th April, 2011, implying a Special Court had been designated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Chief Judge, City Sessions Court, Calcutta had the jurisdiction to pass the order dated 7th April, 2022.
appellant_arguments: Since no Special Court had been constituted by the State Government under Section 22(1) of the NIA Act, the Sessions Court had exclusive jurisdiction to try the offences as per Section 22(3) of the NIA Act.
respondent_arguments: The view taken by the High Court, which interfered with the order dated 7th April, 2022, was the only permissible and legal view, suggesting the court lacked jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order dated 07.04.2022, whereby the Chief Judge cum City Sessions Court permitted the addition of the offences under Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 to the case suffer from any illegality or infirmity; whether the extension of remand by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate beyond the period of 90 days was illegal.
appellant_arguments: Since the accused never filed an application seeking default bail after the expiry of 90 days and before the filing of the charge sheet, any irregularity in the matter of granting remand was cured.
The accused has lost the right to claim release on default bail.
respondent_arguments: The view taken by the High Court, which interfered with the order dated 7th April, 2022, was the only permissible and legal view, implying the order and the extension of remand were illegal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A provision that confers jurisdiction upon a normal criminal court also includes a Special Court constituted under Section 11 or Section 22 of the National Investigation Agency (NIA) Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's judgment was unsustainable and must be reversed. The reasoning, based on the accepted arguments of the appellant, is that because the State of West Bengal had not notified a Special Court under Section 22(1) of the NIA Act, the Sessions Court was vested with exclusive jurisdiction to try the offences and, consequently, to entertain applications for the extension of remand under the UAPA, as stipulated by Section 22(3) of the NIA Act.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of the National Investigating Agency Act, 2008, specifically analyzing the relationship between Section 22(1), which allows a State Government to designate a Court of Session as a Special Court, and Section 22(3), which grants jurisdiction to the Court of Session for the relevant area in cases where no such Special Court has been designated.
